children.text: DOPPLER LASER COOLING AND OPTICAL MOLASSES

A two-level atom of mass m moves along +x with speed v. Ground-state internal energy is zero and excited-state energy is \(\hbar\omega_0\). A laser photon travels along -x with laboratory frequency \(\omega_L\), energy \(\hbar\omega_L\), and momentum \(-\hbar q\), where \(q=\omega_L/c>0\). Assume \(v/c\ll1\) and \(\hbar q/(mv)\ll1\). Keep first-order corrections appropriate to the observable and discard their products. Absorption is followed by spontaneous emission with equal probability along either x direction. Part I uses a resonant incident beam. All atomic energies exclude the constant rest energy.

statement.text:
DOPPLER LASER COOLING AND OPTICAL MOLASSES
A two-level atom of mass m moves along +x with speed v. Ground-state internal energy is zero and excited-state energy is \(\hbar\omega_0\). A laser photon travels along -x with laboratory frequency \(\omega_L\), energy \(\hbar\omega_L\), and momentum \(-\hbar q\), where \(q=\omega_L/c>0\). Assume \(v/c\ll1\) and \(\hbar q/(mv)\ll1\). Keep first-order corrections appropriate to the observable and discard their products. Absorption is followed by spontaneous emission with equal probability along either x direction. Part I uses a resonant incident beam. All atomic energies exclude the constant rest energy.

1a. Absorption resonance
Write the resonance condition for the counterpropagating photon.
1b. Momentum after absorption
Find the atomic laboratory momentum immediately after absorption.
1c. Energy after absorption
Find total atomic kinetic plus internal energy after absorption.
2a. Backward photon energy
If the spontaneous photon is emitted along -x, find its laboratory energy.
2b. Backward photon momentum
Find that emitted photon's signed laboratory momentum.
2c. Atom after backward emission
Find the final atom momentum for this emission direction.
2d. Atom energy after backward emission
Find its final energy after backward emission.
3a. Forward photon energy
If emission is along +x, find the photon's laboratory energy.
3b. Forward photon momentum
Find the forward photon momentum, retaining its first-order Doppler correction.
3c. Atom after forward emission
Find the final atomic momentum at the stipulated atomic-momentum order.
3d. Atom energy after forward emission
Find the final atomic energy consistently with momentum and energy conservation.
4a. Mean emitted photon energy
Average the two equally likely photon energies.
4b. Mean emitted photon momentum
Find its mean momentum at the retained order relative to the atomic momentum.
4c. Mean final atomic energy
Find mean atomic energy after emission.
4d. Mean final atomic momentum
Find the mean final atomic momentum.
5a. Mean energy transfer
Find the mean atomic energy change in one complete absorption-emission cycle.
5b. Mean momentum transfer
Find the mean atomic momentum change in one complete cycle.
6a. Co-propagating energy transfer
Now a resonant laser beam of laboratory frequency \(\omega_L^{\prime}\) travels along +x with the atom. Find mean energy change per cycle.
6b. Co-propagating momentum transfer
Find mean momentum change per co-propagating cycle.
7a. Two-beam force

For N atoms at rest, a beam produces excited population \(N_{exc}=N\Omega_R^2/[(\omega_0-\omega_L)^2+\Gamma^2/4+2\Omega_R^2]\), with lifetime \(\Gamma^{-1}\). Thus cycles occur at rate \(\Gamma N_{exc}\). Two opposite beams of the same arbitrary frequency illuminate atoms moving at v. Find their total force, treating the two beam rates independently in this supplied model.
8a. Linear friction force
Expand the two-beam force to first order in v.
8b. Positive force condition
For \(v>0\), when does the force speed up the atoms?
8c. Zero force condition
When is the force zero for the symmetric pair?
8d. Cooling condition
For \(v>0\), when does the force slow the atoms?
8e. Cooling for opposite motion
If the atoms instead move at velocity \(-v\), what detuning gives cooling?
9a. Velocity decay
For red detuning and initial velocity \(v_0\), find velocity after time \(\tau\). Use b for the per-atom coefficient defined in 8a.
9b. Temperature decay
The atoms initially have thermal equilibrium temperature \(T_0\). Find their temperature after time tau in this deterministic low-velocity model.

children.text: DOPPLER LASER COOLING AND OPTICAL MOLASSES
The approaching atom sees a blueshift: \(\omega_0=\omega_L(1+v/c)\) to first order.
Energy conservation gives \(E_{at}=mv^2/2+\hbar\omega_L\). Equivalently, \((mv-\hbar q)^2/(2m)+\hbar\omega_0\) reduces to this at the retained order.
Backward Doppler redshift cancels the incident resonance blueshift, leaving \(E_\gamma\simeq\hbar\omega_L\).
The emitted backward momentum restores the incident loss: \(p_{at}=mv\) to retained order.
The atom returns to its internal ground state and original momentum, so \(E_{at}=mv^2/2\).
The emitted light is Doppler blueshifted in addition to the incident resonance shift: \(E_\gamma=\hbar\omega_L(1+2v/c)\).
\(p_{at}=mv-2\hbar q\). The extra photon Doppler term is a product of the two small ratios when compared with mv, so it is discarded here.

Expand \((mv-2\hbar q)^2/(2m)\) to first order in recoil relative to mv: \[E_{at}=\frac12mv^2-2\hbar qv.\] This also follows from 1c minus 3a. The official solution's corresponding expression loses a factor two in the kinetic-energy change. The native key uses the conservation-consistent result.
The residual \(\hbar qv/c\) is a product of the two small ratios relative to mv, so the retained mean emitted momentum is zero.
Average 2d and the corrected 3d: \[\overline E_{at}=mv^2/2-\hbar qv.\] The source's half-sized average loss inherits the factor error in 3d.
Average mv and \(mv-2\hbar q\), yielding \(mv-\hbar q\).

\[\Delta E=-\hbar qv=-\hbar\omega_Lv/c.\] It equals v times mean momentum transfer to the retained order. The official answer has an erroneous factor one half, inconsistent with both conservation and 5b.

The resonance condition is \(\omega_0=\omega_L^{\prime}(1-v/c)\). Reversing the photon momentum reverses the first-order work, giving \(\Delta E=+\hbar\omega_L^{\prime}v/c\). This corrects the same factor-one-half error in the official answer.

Let \(\delta=\omega_0-\omega_L\), \(q=\omega_L/c\), \(D=\Gamma^2/4+2\Omega_R^2\). The +x beam is seen at \(\omega_L-qv\), and the -x beam at \(\omega_L+qv\). Thus \[F=N\Gamma\hbar q\Omega_R^2\left[\frac1{(\delta+qv)^2+D}-\frac1{(\delta-qv)^2+D}\right].\]

Writing \(D_0=\delta^2+\Gamma^2/4+2\Omega_R^2\), the denominator difference is \(-4\delta qv/D_0^2\). Hence \[F=-Nbv,\qquad b=\frac{4\hbar q^2\Omega_R^2\Gamma\delta}{D_0^2}.\] Here b is the damping coefficient per atom, not the total coefficient Nb.
Blue detuning, \(\omega_L>\omega_0\), gives \(\delta<0\) and positive force.
At exact resonance \(\omega_L=\omega_0\), the two rates are equal. The force is also zero at v = 0 for any detuning.
Red detuning, \(\omega_L<\omega_0\), gives positive b and a force opposite to v.
The linear force is odd in v. The same red-detuning condition \(\omega_L<\omega_0\) gives a force opposing either velocity sign.
Total mass is Nm, so \(Nm\dot v=-Nbv\). Therefore \[v(\tau)=v_0e^{-b\tau/m}.\] Dividing a total force coefficient by the single-atom mass without cancelling N would be inconsistent.

Every velocity component in the one-dimensional model is reduced by \(e^{-b\tau/m}\). Since temperature is proportional to mean-square velocity, \[T(\tau)=T_0e^{-2b\tau/m}.\] Recoil diffusion and other heating prevent the model from describing arbitrarily low temperatures.

solution.text:
DOPPLER LASER COOLING AND OPTICAL MOLASSES
1a. Absorption resonance
The approaching atom sees a blueshift: \(\omega_0=\omega_L(1+v/c)\) to first order.
1b. Momentum after absorption
Conserve momentum: \(p_{at}=mv-\hbar q\).
1c. Energy after absorption
Energy conservation gives \(E_{at}=mv^2/2+\hbar\omega_L\). Equivalently, \((mv-\hbar q)^2/(2m)+\hbar\omega_0\) reduces to this at the retained order.
2a. Backward photon energy
Backward Doppler redshift cancels the incident resonance blueshift, leaving \(E_\gamma\simeq\hbar\omega_L\).
2b. Backward photon momentum
\(p_\gamma=-\hbar\omega_L/c=-\hbar q\).
2c. Atom after backward emission
The emitted backward momentum restores the incident loss: \(p_{at}=mv\) to retained order.
2d. Atom energy after backward emission
The atom returns to its internal ground state and original momentum, so \(E_{at}=mv^2/2\).
3a. Forward photon energy
The emitted light is Doppler blueshifted in addition to the incident resonance shift: \(E_\gamma=\hbar\omega_L(1+2v/c)\).
3b. Forward photon momentum
\(p_\gamma=E_\gamma/c=\hbar\omega_L(1+2v/c)/c\).
3c. Atom after forward emission
\(p_{at}=mv-2\hbar q\). The extra photon Doppler term is a product of the two small ratios when compared with mv, so it is discarded here.
3d. Atom energy after forward emission
Expand \((mv-2\hbar q)^2/(2m)\) to first order in recoil relative to mv: \[E_{at}=\frac12mv^2-2\hbar qv.\] This also follows from 1c minus 3a. The official solution's corresponding expression loses a factor two in the kinetic-energy change. The native key uses the conservation-consistent result.
4a. Mean emitted photon energy
\(\overline E_\gamma=\hbar\omega_L(1+v/c)\).
4b. Mean emitted photon momentum
The residual \(\hbar qv/c\) is a product of the two small ratios relative to mv, so the retained mean emitted momentum is zero.
4c. Mean final atomic energy
Average 2d and the corrected 3d: \[\overline E_{at}=mv^2/2-\hbar qv.\] The source's half-sized average loss inherits the factor error in 3d.
4d. Mean final atomic momentum
Average mv and \(mv-2\hbar q\), yielding \(mv-\hbar q\).
5a. Mean energy transfer
\[\Delta E=-\hbar qv=-\hbar\omega_Lv/c.\] It equals v times mean momentum transfer to the retained order. The official answer has an erroneous factor one half, inconsistent with both conservation and 5b.
5b. Mean momentum transfer
\(\Delta p=-\hbar q\).
6a. Co-propagating energy transfer
The resonance condition is \(\omega_0=\omega_L^{\prime}(1-v/c)\). Reversing the photon momentum reverses the first-order work, giving \(\Delta E=+\hbar\omega_L^{\prime}v/c\). This corrects the same factor-one-half error in the official answer.
6b. Co-propagating momentum transfer
\(\Delta p=+\hbar\omega_L^{\prime}/c\).
7a. Two-beam force
Let \(\delta=\omega_0-\omega_L\), \(q=\omega_L/c\), \(D=\Gamma^2/4+2\Omega_R^2\). The +x beam is seen at \(\omega_L-qv\), and the -x beam at \(\omega_L+qv\). Thus \[F=N\Gamma\hbar q\Omega_R^2\left[\frac1{(\delta+qv)^2+D}-\frac1{(\delta-qv)^2+D}\right].\]
8a. Linear friction force
Writing \(D_0=\delta^2+\Gamma^2/4+2\Omega_R^2\), the denominator difference is \(-4\delta qv/D_0^2\). Hence \[F=-Nbv,\qquad b=\frac{4\hbar q^2\Omega_R^2\Gamma\delta}{D_0^2}.\] Here b is the damping coefficient per atom, not the total coefficient Nb.
8b. Positive force condition
Blue detuning, \(\omega_L>\omega_0\), gives \(\delta<0\) and positive force.
8c. Zero force condition
At exact resonance \(\omega_L=\omega_0\), the two rates are equal. The force is also zero at v = 0 for any detuning.
8d. Cooling condition
Red detuning, \(\omega_L<\omega_0\), gives positive b and a force opposite to v.
8e. Cooling for opposite motion
The linear force is odd in v. The same red-detuning condition \(\omega_L<\omega_0\) gives a force opposing either velocity sign.
9a. Velocity decay
Total mass is Nm, so \(Nm\dot v=-Nbv\). Therefore \[v(\tau)=v_0e^{-b\tau/m}.\] Dividing a total force coefficient by the single-atom mass without cancelling N would be inconsistent.
9b. Temperature decay
Every velocity component in the one-dimensional model is reduced by \(e^{-b\tau/m}\). Since temperature is proportional to mean-square velocity, \[T(\tau)=T_0e^{-2b\tau/m}.\] Recoil diffusion and other heating prevent the model from describing arbitrarily low temperatures.
